1772.heavy: Final syllable attracts stress only when it 'contains a long vowel and is closed by a single consonant' (CVVC) or 'is closed by a cluster of two consonants' (CVCC); a final closed by a single consonant after a short vowel (CVC, e.g. tə́kməl) does not attract stress.
1772.dflt: penult ('the penultimate syllable is stressed in all other cases'); monosyllables trivially stressed
1772.prule: Isolated word: stress the final syllable if it is superheavy, i.e. CVVC (long vowel + one closing consonant) or CVCC (closed by a two-consonant cluster); otherwise stress the penultimate syllable, whether the final is open (CV) or closed CVC. Stress is mobile: it is recomputed on the surface syllable structure after affixation/negation circumfix (mā...-š).

1773.prule: No word-stress rule is stated in any reachable source. Holm (1914: 28) gives only an impressionistic comparison with West Greenlandic: Angmagsalik speakers 'often stress the final syllables of the words and pronounce them with a higher pitch'. Thalbitzer's 1923 phonetic description of the Ammassalik dialect (sections Consonants, Vowels, Quantity, Assimilation) has no accent/stress section; stress appears only as (i) a 'moving of the stress' during inflection/suffixation that conditions consonant gradation (§32, §34) and (ii) a remark that the 'dynamic accent' keeps 'constantly shifting the pronunciation of the words, not the least in the accentuation of the long words' (p. 175). Robbe & Dorais 1986 Tunumiit oraasiat (the WALS 'gre' source) WAS reached (archive.org full text): its 'Phonology and orthography' outline (intro pp. xx-xxi) treats vowel harmony, intervocalic lenition, cluster correspondences and orthography and contains no statement on stress, accent, pitch or intonation. Mennecier 1995 Le tunumiisut and Dorais 2010 were not reachable.

1775.dloc: Anchieta 1595, Cap. III 'De Accentu' and 'Do Cremento', p. 10-11 of the 1874 Platzmann edition (archive.org)
1775.prule: Accent falls on the last syllable of the base (stem): all words ending in e/i/o/u are final-accented; verbs are mostly final-accented whatever consonant or vowel they end in (ajucá, amondéb); a-final nouns split between final (tatá) and penult (óca) [= modern analysis ók-a, consonant-final stem + always-unstressed nominal suffix -a]; apparent penults in -e are compounds with an enclitic monosyllabic postposition (icatú-pe); V+i / V+u finals are diphthongs (acái, xeéu). Under suffixation ('cremento') the base keeps its 'accento natural' (óca/ócamo, tatá/tatáne/tatáreme); only polysyllabic increments with a 'long penult' carry the accent themselves (tataráma, ocoéra); grave-marked final monosyllables in cremento/composition are enclitics that leave the base accent in place (çó-reme-nhè).
1775.srule: Only in composition: Anchieta says a verb keeps its 'accento natural' and a second accent may be put on a separable tense increment, and (1595 ed. fol. 9) that in compounds each member may keep its own accent (óka + katú > okatú); grave-marked monosyllabic enclitics (-pè, -nhè, as in çóreme-nhè, çóreme-nhè-pè) leave the base accent in place, as do short-penult increments such as -reme (tatáreme). No rhythmic secondary stress is described. Rodrigues 1958 restates: compounds and words derived with tonic suffixes (-sáb-a, -pýr-a) carry one intensity accent per member; simple words have one accent.

1776.prule: No word-stress rule. Turkana is described as a tone language: every vowel carries H or L (plus downstep/downdrift; Vossen 1982 after Heine 1980b: two level tones and a high-falling contour). Dimmendaal 1983 adds word-level pitch tendencies (lowering of word-final tones, raising of non-initial tones; a 'pitch-accent rule' inserting L on the second mora of certain nouns, pp. 236-237) which he labels 'pitch-accent'/'musical stress' after Hyman 1975 and explicitly distinguishes from stress accent/dynamic stress; Dimmendaal 2012 declines to posit word-level accent and links tone melodies to bimoraic foot structure instead.

Vossen 1982: tone significant lexically and grammatically; Heine 1980b two level tones + HL contour vs Polley & Jeffrey three tonemes. Barrett 1988 (non-linguist) gives hedged word-'accent' tendencies (final in disyllables; final or penult in trisyllables; generally final in 4+), best read as an impression of the tonal/pitch-accent pattern, not a stress rule.

One secondary per word as described (no iteration stated).

1778.prule: Two phonemic tones (H marked, L unmarked); every phonological word carries exactly one H, which may fall on any syllable (lexically contrastive: /díi/ 'blood' vs /dií/ 'mud'; in 3+ syllable words H on any syllable). Stress ('acento') is a concomitant feature of the H toneme, i.e. prominence sits wherever the lexical H is; no positional stress rule. Sub-regularity: disyllabic (C)VCV words have H on the second syllable, except loanwords.
1778.srule: None: one prominence per word -- 'La palabra fonológica tiene un tono alto, y sólo uno.... El acento es un rasgo concomitante del tonema alto.' 1778.tone: Source treats the system as tone (H vs L) with a culminative constraint: one and only one H per phonological word, position free/contrastive; 'El acento es un rasgo concomitante del tonema alto' — stress is derivative of the H tone, not independently placed. tn.translation: There are two phonemic tones: high /´/ and low (unmarked). The phonological word has one high tone, and only one. It may occur on any syllable of the word. The low tone has two variants: a mid tone [-] ... and a low tone [`] which occurs elsewhere. Stress is a concomitant feature of the high toneme. ... Tone is contrastive in two-syllable words of the shape (C)VV. /díi/ 'blood' /dií/ 'mud' ... A pattern of terraced tonal descent occurs in words and phrases of three or more syllables, with the result that each high/low grouping is lower than the preceding high/low grouping.

1780.dq: Mainly, it is the stress patterns described in 4.6 which help us define words. Secondary stress can only be assigned to a word-initial syllable. Primary stress is assigned to the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable of underived words, unless there is a diphthong (see 4.6.1), or otherwise as specified by lexical rules (4.6.3-4.6.6), where affixes give stress shifts. (sec. 4.7 'The word', p. 47)

1780.heavy: diphthongs: 'In words with diphthongs, the diphthong in the rightmost foot always gets primary stress.' All syllables are open (no codas), vowel length not distinctive.
1780.dflt: lexically penult or antepenult (no single default stated)
1780.prule: Primary stress on the penult OR the antepenult of the root; which of the two is lexically determined per word (not predictable, but stress is stated to be non-distinctive). Disyllables: penult (antepenult n.a.). Monosyllables stressed. Diphthong in the rightmost foot always takes primary stress (incl. word-final, e.g. pa'kao 'goat fish', baka'rao 'frog'). Secondary stress always on the word-initial syllable.
1780.srule: One secondary stress, on the word-initial syllable, whenever the primary is not initial (ˌpaˈzuna, ˌmateˈana, ˌsiˈnipara; initial diphthong ka̯oˈkana): 'Secondary stress is always assigned to the first syllable' (V -> [+stress] / # C0 _); 'Secondary stress can only be assigned to a word-initial syllable'. In derived words the prefix/reduplicant carries it; in RED + -a(i)ni nominalizations it is on the second syllable = first syllable of the base (ma ˌmaruvuˈaini). No alternating/rhythmic stresses described.
1780.quote: One-syllable words get primary stress on their only syllable. Generally speaking, there are two primary stress patterns for word roots with more than two syllables. However, stress is influenced by the presence of diphthongs, as will be seen further below. It is lexically determined which words each of the stress rules below apply to. morph.elicq: No statement of how stress was determined. Nearest: Ch.4 intro (p.35): "This chapter gives a short introduction to phonological units, stress patterns and phonological rules in Ughele. The strings of language are described in a canonical phonemic transcription, separating each word as if the words had been spoken one at a time, isolated from the context of preceding and following words. ... Fine phonetic detail is not addressed." Corpus overall (§3.1 p.27): "The data this thesis is based on consist of elicited and natural speech, about half of which is recorded on audio or video." No instrumental measurements or frames are mentioned for stress.
morph.stmt: Ughele has little bound inflection and its affixes are "mostly derivational" (Ch.6 p.69): valency-changing verb derivation is prefixal ("There are three derivational prefixes, the causative prefix va-, the distributive prefix vari-, and the passive prefix ta-", §12.2 p.157) and nominalisation sits at the left edge (infix <in>, prefix ara-, CV- reduplication), while transitivity (-i/-ni), object indexing (enclitics) and possessor/attributive indexing (-gu/-na/-di etc.) follow the stem; tense is absent and aspect, mood, negation, articles and subject markers are free preverbal/prenominal particles ("Aspect and mood are expressed through preverbal particles…

dfl.q: Generally speaking, there are two primary stress patterns for word roots with more than two syllables. Primary stress is assigned to the penultimate (a) or antepenultimate (b) syllable. Stress is not a distinctive feature in Ughele, and there is no set of vowels that trigger one or the other stress pattern. ... It is lexically determined which words each of the stress rules below apply to.

1781.dq: Word stress is free in Ukrainian (Brovčenko 1969). ... The main stress can appear on any syllable in a given word ... [separate section 'Intonation'] Words are parsed into phrases or the so-called accent units in which the last word is usually accented. A rising-falling or falling intonation is characteristic of the main stressed syllable.
1781.dloc: JIPA 47(3), section 'Syllable structure and word stress' (pp. 349-357; Cambridge Core full-text HTML); De Bray 1969 p.74 'Pronunciation'
1781.prule: Free (lexical) word stress: main stress may fall on any syllable of the word, is contrastive (minimal pairs), and is mobile within inflectional paradigms; sensitive to morphology. No weight or positional rule.
1781.srule: primary source (Pompino-Marschall et al. 2017): words of four or more syllables may carry an optional secondary stress, never adjacent to the primary; no placement pattern agreed (after Zilyns'kyj 1979: 187-190). Superseded by the acoustic studies of Łukaszewicz & Mołczanow (2018 JoL; Mołczanow et al. 2018 SP: 908, 911; Łukaszewicz & Mołczanow 2024 SP: 285, 288): predictable rhythmic secondary stresses at both word edges (word-initial and word-final syllables) iterating towards the lexical stress and never adjacent to it, e.g. [ˌσσˈσσ], [σˈσσˌσ], [ˈσσˌσ], [ˌσσˈσ], [ˌʋɛlɔˌsɨpɛˈdɨst], [ˈlaɦɔˌdɨtɨˌmɛ], [ˌmatɛmaˈtɨčnɔˌɦɔ]; cued by vowel duration only (speakers from Western Ukraine).
1781.quote: Word stress is free in Ukrainian (Brovčenko 1969). morph.stmt: Umbrian is an inflecting, overwhelmingly suffixing Italic language of Latin type -- 'we can maintain that the Latin inflectional system as a whole is also the Italic' (Buck 1904 sec. 18): case/number, person, tense, mood and voice are all marked by endings after the stem, the only prefixal layer being derivational preverbs ('The only extensive type of verbal composition is that in which the first element is an adverbial prefix', sec. 264.1) plus the privative an- and rare perfect reduplication, while post-stem material is further extended by enclitic postpositions ('The enclitic use of prepositions is far more common than in Latin', sec. 165.2: tota-per, fesnaf-e, akru-tu, esunes-ku).

1785.dq: Words are usually polysyllabic, and the accent falls, as a rule, upon the penultimate
1785.prule: Word accent on the penultimate syllable 'as a rule' (Stover 1885 sec. 18; Nascimento 1894 'em regra, sobre a penultima syllaba'), with every full vowel counted as a syllable nucleus and prevocalic i/u (w, y) as glides. Stover's two stated deviations reduce to this count: (i) word-final vowel combinations (ai, ae, au...) 'accent the ultima' but this 'is only an apparent exception; really the accent falls on the stronger vowel' = the penultimate vowel, and Nascimento states outright that such combinations 'contam se por duas syllabas... Teem o acccnto tonico na penultima vogal. Ex.: ukai' (and, word-medially before a consonant, on their last vowel = again the word's penultimate vowel); (ii) 'if the penultimate contains a semi-vowel, the accent goes to the antepenult' is exemplified only by the expanded spelling chi-lu-wa 'accent on the antepenult' = surface chi.lwa, i.e. penult once w/y are 'treated as full consonants' as Stover's own orthography does; Nascimento drops this clause ('i e u antes de qualquer vogal sao semi-vogaes'). quantity-insensitive; no morphological conditioning stated.

tn.quote: Tone: There are two tones: H(igh) and L(ow). A word can also contain floating tones, i.e., tones which are not Unked to any vowel. There are only Low floating tones m surface representations, and they only occur between High tones. These tones are pronounced according to the following rules: (a) A floating Low tone lowers the pitch of all following High tones. (b) A floating Low tone immediately before the last syllable of a word … The last-but-one syllable is realized as falling from High to downstepp>ed-High, and the last syllable remains on that same level of downstepped-High.

1787.prule: Primary stress (tryck + accent, marked /ˈ/) on the first syllable of the word = first syllable of the first foot; feet are 2-3 syllables, trochaic (first syllable of every foot stressed); later feet (in compounds, certain derivations, and certain inflectional endings analysed as their own foot, e.g. superlative /mʉs/, Kom.Pl /jˌkʉjmə/; abessive forms in /htaah/ are analysed as two-footed with the ending's /aa/ as latus, almatjahtáh /ˈalməˌʧahtaah/) carry secondary stress /ˌ/ without accent. No reference to syllable weight for stress placement.
1787.srule: Secondary stress (stress without accent, /ˌ/) on the first syllable of every non-initial foot; additional feet arise in compounds, certain derivations and certain inflectional suffixes analysed as their own (sometimes monosyllabic) foot (superlative -mus, Pst.Pl3 -eäh, Kom.Pl -gújme), so placement follows morphological foot structure, not syllable count: árrade /ˈaarrətə/ (one foot, none) vs stuorájmus /ˈstuoraajˌmʉs/ (syllable 3), compound jávuovuossub /ˈjaavuoˌvuossəp/ (syllables 1 and 3).

Vissa böjningar, samt avledningar och sammansättningar kan ge fyra eller fler stavelser, men ord med fler än fem stavelser är sällsynta. Prosodin i umesamiska kommer här analyseras som påverkad av två faktorer: tryck och accent. Den första stavelsen i varje fot har tryck. 1789.dq: 7.2.4. Word Stress ... In words with no long vowels the first vowel is stressed, e.g. táwura. In words with long vowels the the last long vowel is stressed
1789.dloc: sec. 7.2.4 'Word Stress' and sec. 7.2.3 'Consonant Length', p.63 (of the archive.org Rosetta Project excerpt)
1789.heavy: Heavy = a syllable containing a long vowel (aa, ii, uu) only: 'Primary Stress occurs on the last long vowel' (sec. 2.4.2, p. 6); 'In words with no long vowels the first vowel is stressed' (sec. 7.2.4, p. 63). Short-vowel closed syllables do not attract stress: in the p. 6 examples káchìnpinta 'female', pím'ìntaka 'hawk', tángkàltangangka 'keeps aching' and pìtalpitáanchimangka 'always understanding' primary stress stays on the first vowel or on the long vowel, never on a short closed syllable. In words without long vowels the consonant after the stressed first vowel is lengthened (pama -> pámma, secs. 2.3 and 7.2.3); a long vowel does not occur in a word-final CV syllable (sec. 2.5.1, p. 7).
1789.prule: Stress the last (rightmost) long vowel of the word; if the word has no long vowel, stress the first vowel (initial syllable), with the following consonant lengthened (pama -> pámma).
1789.srule: One secondary stress per word: in words without long vowels, on the second vowel (pámà, káyìna); in words with long vowels, on the long vowel preceding the primary-stressed last long vowel if there is one (wàacháaya, mùumáanya), otherwise on the first vowel of the word (pìtáanchimana, tàwuráalu). 'Predictable, but not rigid': emphasis, mood and fast speech often equalise or reverse primary and secondary stress.
1789.quote: 7.2.3. Consonant Length Some consonants are sounded long. This always happens in a word with no long vowels. In these words the first syllable is stressed and the next consonant is sounded long. For example, pama is sounded: pámma A second m is not put in writing because language speakers always say it that way. 7.2.4. Word Stress (see 2.4. on page 6 for more detail) In words with no long vowels the first vowel is stressed, e.g. táwura. In words with long vowels the the last long vowel is stressed, e.g. páala, muumáanya, pitáanchi, tawuráalu.
1789.loc: sec. 7.2.4 'Word Stress' and sec. 7.2.3 'Consonant Length', p.63 (of the archive.org Rosetta Project excerpt)

1789.exq_: Kuuku Ya'u and Umpila have predictable, but not rigid, primary and secondary stress patterns. The stress is quite readily affected by emphasis, mood, fast speech etc., and frequently the effect is to equalise or reverse primary and secondary stress.

1792.dq: Word stress is predictable and so does not need to be represented phonemically. Clause stress falls on the last syllable of the last word in the clause.
1792.heavy: Stressable = major or minor syllable with a full vowel; pre-syllable (C(C)V with only the vocalic transition /e/ [ə], never a final consonant) cannot bear stress.
1792.prule: Main word stress on the penultimate syllable (minor stress on the final); if the penult is a pre-syllable (C(C) + schwa-like vocalic transition /e/, never closed), it is unstressed and main stress falls on the final syllable. Compounds/reduplications: each member keeps its stress, the last one is major.
1792.srule: Minor (secondary) stress on the final syllable when main stress is penultimate; pre-syllables carry no stress. In trisyllables whose first syllable is the prefix ber-/per-/ter- ([Cer-] allomorph) that syllable has an optional minor stress, normal phrase-finally and lost in fast speech (e.g. 'Minor + Pre-syllable + Major' permelaw 'word': minor on the first, major on the last). In compounds and reduplications each component keeps its stress, the last being major and the preceding ones minor; minor stresses may weaken in rapid speech.
1792.quote: In normal speech the main word stress falls on the penultimate syllable, as in Malay, with minor stress on the final syllable (Lewis 1947:18). evidence_works.detail: In six trisyllabic all-/a:/ words the authors find three stress levels separated most reliably by vowel duration, with main stress on a super-heavy (CVVC) syllable where one exists (the last one when there are two: nasazgar, khaksaran; the initial one in karkhana; the medial one in amajga), on the penult when all three syllables are CVV (pajama), and secondary stress on another heavy syllable.
